statement: Schedule 2 strength sessions per week by default; allow 3 for athletes with a lifting background in a base or general phase; never exceed 3. Do not raise frequency to chase additional benefit.
appliesTo: All distance runners, 5 km to ultra

statement: Run a structured heavy-plus-plyometric block of at least 10 weeks, with 10-14 weeks preferred for heavy resistance; avoid 4-6 week bursts. Benefit increases with duration, but the exact threshold is not established.

Make heavy, low-rep lower-body lifting (80% 1RM or more, with 90% 1RM or more best supported) the primary economy stimulus after a technique base. Use submaximal circuits and isometrics only as support or tissue conditioning; they did not improve economy.
appliesTo: Runners with a technique base; targeting moderate to fast paces

statement: No trial identifies an optimal set and rep scheme. Conservative default: 2-4 lower-body exercises, 3-4 sets of 3-6 repetitions, preceded by a 2-4 week ramp-in of technique and lighter loads. The one trial template is 4 sets of 4RM, three times per week for 8 weeks in 17 runners. Make these values user-configurable.
value: 2-4 exercises x 3-4 sets x 3-6 reps; 2-4 week ramp-in
appliesTo: All runners starting a heavy block

statement: Pair heavy work with plyometrics in the same block. Prioritize plyometrics when target running pace is 12 km/h or slower (long runs, ultra, trail); keep contacts low, with the observed upper end about 200 jumps per session plus 5-10 short sprints. The 200 cap is the maximum observed in trials, not a tested limit.
appliesTo: Runners in a strength block; emphasis for slow-pace and ultra runners

statement: Present expected benefit as a small oxygen-cost improvement (planning figure 2-4% after a complete block; individual studies up to 6-8%), never as a VO2max, threshold or pace change. Treat SMD -1.42 and single-study figures (5-6%) as upper bounds. Derive VO2max and threshold estimates from running data only. In the one women-only randomised trial in the corpus whose abstract reports running economy, 11 weeks of heavy lower-body training raised 1RM by 40% and changed neither running economy nor a 40-minute run, so word the benefit as 'may' and say that the evidence in women is small.

Keep strength in the plan all year. After the main block and during peak-mileage phases drop to 1 maintenance session per week at reduced volume (heavy sets kept, volume cut). The maintenance dose is a design choice: no trial in this corpus tested it. Progress volume and intensity gradually across the year.
appliesTo: All runners after the main block and at peak mileage

statement: Separate plyometric and heavy sessions from key running sessions (long run, intervals) by at least 3 hours, or place them on a different day; place them on easy-run days where possible. Same-session lifting is acceptable for maximal strength goals. Evidence concerns strength outcomes, not running performance.
appliesTo: All runners combining strength and running

statement: Include strength in every plan as a supportive injury-risk measure, but do not state a running-specific injury reduction; sports-general meta-analyses (RR about 0.32-0.34, overuse RR about 0.53) were not confirmed by the one large running RCT (RR 0.97). Do not turn the dose-response figure into a formula.
Do not prescribe static stretching as an injury-prevention measure; spend the time on strength or proprioceptive work. This does not address mobility or comfort goals.

For novice runners and first-time marathoners, rely on gradual mileage progression and adherence as the injury control; a short self-directed bodyweight routine did not reduce overuse injury. Offer strength as a low-cost addition, and cap weekly load increases to guard against bone stress injury.

Use the same strength prescription for masters runners (about 40-50 years): heavy low-rep work is justified and age did not moderate outcomes. As a conservative design choice, lengthen the ramp-in to 4 weeks. No evidence above about 50 years; no female masters evidence.
value: same as general rule; ramp-in 4 weeks

statement: For ultra and trail runners, include a roughly 12-week strength, explosive and plyometric block with plyometric emphasis at slow speeds; use 2 sessions per week (3 optional) and offer a home-based option. Track late-run durability (pace fade, heart rate drift). No evidence exists for 100-mile runners, downhill or eccentric work.
appliesTo: Ultra and trail runners (evidence is from ultra-marathoners and well-trained 10 km runners)

statement: Include explicit calf and plantarflexor strengthening (heavy calf raises) in the lower-body exercise selection; the change in calf-raise 1RM correlated with oxygen-cost change in a small RCT.

Progress each lift by double progression inside its repetition range: raise the load by one step the equipment can make when every set reaches the top of the range with repetitions in reserve and a recorded count, lower it after a set below the range, and hold it otherwise. The closest published convention is a 2-10% increase when the lifter can do the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number; a step larger than 15% of the load is not offered unless it is the smallest step the equipment makes, so a light load can still move. No paper compares ways of progressing a load in runners, so the rule is a default.
value: one step; at most 15% of the load, or the smallest step the equipment makes
appliesTo: Every loaded lift of the strength block

statement: Set the effort of a lift by the repetitions to leave in reserve (1-3 in the block, 3 or more in a ramp-in, a taper and a return), treat the count as imprecise by about one repetition, and never raise a load on a missing count. Strength gains did not depend on the estimated repetitions in reserve over a wide range, so leaving repetitions is not shown to cost strength.
value: 1-3 in the block; 3 or more otherwise

statement: Estimate the one-repetition maximum from submaximal sets, label it an estimate, use it only for a first load, a ceiling and a figure beside a load, and never ask for a maximal attempt. The repetitions possible at a percentage of the maximum vary between people and exercises, and a linear equation was advised only up to 10 repetitions, so a set above 10 repetitions to the limit (done plus left) gives no estimate; no paper validates an equation in runners.
value: linear form with a divisor of 30; none above 10 repetitions to the limit
appliesTo: Strength suggestions and the history view

statement: Keep one light lifting session a week until the race week as a default and not a requirement. No trial tests resistance training in a taper; 8 middle-distance runners kept an economy gain over 4 weeks without explosive strength work, and 14 elite cyclists lost ground against a control group over 8 weeks without strength work.
value: 1 light session a week; none in the race week

statement: Do not change the strength dose by sex, and say that the evidence in women is small and mixed: two small randomised trials of 19 women each found no change in running economy or a 40-minute run in one and a better 5-minute run after prolonged running in the other.

The calf dose and the choice between straight-knee and bent-knee raises are defaults. In 14 untrained adults, standing raises grew the gastrocnemius more and the soleus about as much as seated raises (muscle volume only), and an exhausting calf-raise protocol did not change modelled tibial stress in the next run in 14 recreational runners. No paper gives sets, repetitions, load or tempo for calf raises in runners.

Do not prescribe depth jumps, drops or bounds to recreational runners: the corpus has no dose or bone-stress data for them, and landing force was higher for depth drops from 60 and 90 cm and depth jumps from 90 cm than for a vertical jump in collegiate and national-level power athletes. Use low-amplitude movements on the spot with a graded number of contacts.
value: start at 40 contacts, add 20 every 2 weeks after a completed running week, cap 200
appliesTo: The jump ladder of the strength block

statement: No paper gives injury or technique data for recreational runners starting barbell lifts; injury rates in competitive weightlifting and powerlifting (2.4-3.3 and 1.0-4.4 injuries per 1000 hours of training) are in the range of other non-contact sports. Offer the barbell after a ramp-in on other lifts, ask for no maximal attempt, leave repetitions in reserve in the first session, and make no claim that barbell lifting is safe for runners.
